nameStory: The flutedshell gets its name from the distinctive ridges or 'flutes' that run along its shell surface, much like the vertical grooves carved into classical architecture columns. These raised ribs give the mussel's shell a sculptured, channeled appearance that's unmistakable once you know what to look for.
description: The flutedshell is a freshwater mussel that lives buried in the sandy or muddy bottoms of rivers and streams. Like all mussels, it's a bivalve mollusk with two hinged shells that protect its soft body inside. These medium-sized mussels typically reach 3-4 inches in length and have an elongated, somewhat oval shape. They spend most of their lives partially buried in sediment, filtering tiny particles of food from the water.

idTips.label: Fluted ridges
idTips.description: The shell surface has distinctive raised ribs or ridges running parallel to the growth lines, creating a corrugated texture that you can feel with your fingertip

idTips.label: Shell shape
idTips.description: Elongated and somewhat rectangular when viewed from the side, typically 3-4 times longer than it is tall

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Exterior ranges from yellowish-brown to dark brown, often with darker rays radiating from the hinge area

idTips.label: Interior surface
idTips.description: Inside of shell is typically white to pale pink with a smooth, pearlescent feel

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized mussel, usually 3-4 inches long, fitting comfortably in an adult's palm

habitat: Flutedshells live in clean, flowing rivers and larger streams with sandy or muddy bottoms throughout New England's river systems. They prefer areas with moderate current where they can burrow partially into the sediment while still accessing the flowing water they need for feeding. Look for them in deeper pools and runs of medium to large rivers, often associated with other freshwater mussels.

seasonality.spring: Best time to search for shells along riverbanks as spring floods may wash empty shells ashore. Living mussels are most active as water temperatures rise.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for finding live mussels in shallow water during low flow periods. Wade carefully in rivers to spot the slight depressions they create in sandy bottoms.
seasonality.fall: Mussels begin burrowing deeper as water temperatures drop. Empty shells from summer mortality may be visible along shorelines after autumn rains.
seasonality.winter: Living mussels are buried deep in sediment and nearly impossible to find. Focus on identifying empty shells in museum collections or photos during this season.

funFact: Flutedshells are ecosystem engineers that can filter up to 15 gallons of river water per day through their bodies, removing bacteria, algae, and pollutants - making them living water purification systems that have been cleaning New England's rivers for thousands of years.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other river mussels, but those distinctive fluted ridges are the giveaway - run your finger along the shell surface and you'll feel the raised ribs that other smooth-shelled mussels lack. Remember: 'Fluted means ridged, not smooth.'
contextualKnowledge: With only 3 recorded observations in New England, flutedshells are extremely rare in our region and may be declining due to water pollution and dam construction. If you think you've found one, take photos and contact local naturalists - your discovery could be scientifically important for tracking this uncommon species.
compareHints: The flutedshell differs from its relative the creek heelsplitter by having those diagnostic fluted ridges, while the heelsplitter has a smoother shell surface. Creek heelsplitters also tend to prefer smaller streams and have a more compressed, thinner shell profile. Both species are uncommon in New England, making any mussel find worth documenting carefully.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The creek heelsplitter differs from its relative the flutedshell by being much more compressed and lacking the prominent ridges or 'flutes' that give its cousin its name.
